 Wage hike must not burden SMEs: DUBS
 Noor Syahhira Hady 
 Business , Top Story 
 02/10/2026 
 6:28 pm

 KUCHING : Any minimum wage increase should be gradual and sustainable, with SME support considered if the adjustment is significant, Datuk Abang Helmi Ikhwan says.
 The Sarawak Bumiputera Entrepreneurs Chamber (DUBS) president said the association welcomed the Federal Government’s ongoing review of the national minimum wage and recognised the importance of ensuring workers received fair and reasonable wages in line with the rising cost of living.
 At the same time, he said any increase should be implemented in a balanced, gradual and sustainable manner, taking into account the capacity of businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs).
 He noted that figures of RM2,000, RM2,100 and RM2,200 had been mentioned in public discussions, although the government had yet to make a final decision.
 “The discussion should therefore focus not only on the amount, but also on the sustainability and wider impact of the policy.
 “For many SMEs, higher wages would also mean higher statutory contributions and operating costs, including logistics, utilities, rentals and other business expenses.
 “Labour-intensive businesses operating on relatively narrow margins could face greater pressure,” he told Sarawak Tribune.
 He also urged the government to take Sarawak’s economic and geographical circumstances into account when reviewing the minimum wage.
 Abang Helmi said logistics costs, geographical distances, labour availability and differences between urban and rural areas could affect the ability of businesses to absorb higher labour costs.
 “If a significant increase is introduced, appropriate transitional support and targeted assistance for affected SMEs should also be considered to help businesses adapt without compromising employment.”
 Abang Helmi also said sustainable wage growth should go hand in hand with higher productivity as Malaysia seeks to become a higher-income economy.
 “Greater emphasis should therefore be placed on skills development, technical and vocational education and training (TVET), digitalisation, automation and technology adoption.”
 He said these measures would enable businesses to generate greater value while providing better wages and career opportunities for workers.
 He pointed out that DUBS also maintained that employers and employees ultimately shared a common interest in a stronger and more sustainable economy.
 “Workers need better incomes and quality employment, while businesses need an environment that enables them to remain competitive, grow and create jobs,” he said.
 He said the objective should be to achieve better wages without undermining business sustainability and employment opportunities.
 “DUBS stood ready to engage with the Federal and Sarawak governments and other stakeholders to contribute to a minimum wage policy that is fair to workers, practical for businesses and sustainable for the economy.”
